sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: How multimodal language models should encode visual input remains up for debate. Most models use a pretrained vision encoder, while some recent recipes train the encoder from scratch with the language model or remove it entirely. Vision encoders bundle together three design choices: a visual prior from upstream pretraining, dedicated vision capacity, and pre-fusion placement of that capacity (i.e., before the multimodal backbone). Because published models also differ in data, architecture, and compute, comparing them cannot isolate the effect of each choice. We disentangle these choices via a controlled framework where we pretrain all models from scratch on common data and compare them on visual question answering and language benchmarks at matched lifetime compute. We find that the visual prior is not necessary; an encoder trained jointly from scratch is on par with a pretrained one, without a separate training stage. What matters instead is dedicated vision capacity: an encoder-free model trails on visual understanding even when its backbone is enlarged by the encoder's parameter count. Yet that capacity need not precede multimodal fusion, as vision-only modules added in-fusion to early backbone layers perform comparably to a pre-fusion encoder and can lower time to first token. These results also hold across backbone sizes, when encoder pretraining is treated as free, and when starting from a pretrained language model. Overall, our findings favor dedicated vision capacity trained jointly with the backbone and placed early within it.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Most multimodal models acquire visual understanding from vision encoder pretrained for separate objective, such as image recognition or imagetext alignment, rather than from being trained directly with the multimodal backbone that uses its features (He et al., 2016; Radford et al., 2021; Tschannen et al., 2025; Siméoni et al., 2026; Tschannen et al., 2023). Multimodal training has progressed from freezing this encoder (Alayrac et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023b; Liu et al., 2023; Muse Glimmer Team, 2026) to updating it (Beyer et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2025a), but encoder pretraining has remained separate stage. Recent recipes bring vision and language closer by discarding parts of the pretrained encoder setup: Kimi K3 trains vision encoder from scratch jointly with the multimodal backbone (Kimi Team, 2026b), and encoder-free models directly process pixel patches, forcing visual encoding to be learned entirely within the backbone (Adept AI, 2023; Diao et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2026; Gemma Team, 2026; Thinking Machines Lab, 2026a). Each recipe implies different answer to what the vision encoder contributes, if anything at all. We ask which of its inherited design choices benefit multimodal models trained entirely from scratch. The predominant multimodal vision encoding recipes bundle together three design choices: (i) visual prior from upstream pretraining, (ii) dedicated vision capacity (i.e., parameters that only vision tokens use), and (iii) pre-fusion placement of that capacity in separate encoder that operates before vision and text tokens interact in the backbonerather than operating in-fusion, within the shared backbone. pretrained encoder keeps all three, from-scratch encoder gives up only the prior, and an encoder-free model gives up all three. Existing comparisons cannot isolate these choices, for two reasons. First, they entangle the choices with each other and the rest of the recipe. Published models differ in data, training stages, compute, and architecture. While controlled studies hold multimodal training data and compute fixed, their comparisons among pretrained encoders (McKinzie et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2024a; Fan et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025) vary which visual prior an encoder imports rather than whether it needs one in the first place. Studies of encoder-based vs. encoder-free models either change all three choices (Tong et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026) or change capacity and placement together (Shukor et al., 2025). Second, comparisons with pretrained encoders control only multimodal training, treating encoder pretraining as free even though it adds substantial compute and data of its own (e.g., SigLIP 2 trains on 40B imagetext samples; Tschannen et al., 2025), and several studies attribute the encoders advantage to its pretraining (Lei et al., 2025; Diao et al., 2025). In this work, we conduct controlled study that unbundles the design choices of multimodal vision encoding one at time (Figure 1): (i) does the vision encoder need separate pretraining? (ii) does vision encoding need dedicated capacity? and (iii) does that capacity need to precede multimodal fusion? We train every model entirely from scratch, language backbone included, on common pool of data with one encoder architecture, one dense backbone architecture, and one optimization recipe. We evaluate models on downstream visual question-answering (VQA) and language benchmarks at backbone sizes from 0.6B to 6.4B. Because recipes spend compute in different stages, we compare them at matched lifetime compute: the total compute of all training stages, including any pretraining of the encoder or language model. Our experiments answer these questions and test whether the answers hold beyond lifetime compute: 1. Separate pretraining is optional (3). At matched lifetime compute, from-scratch encoder is on par with encoders pretrained on the same data. Even if we ignore upstream compute (6.1), more encoder pretraining improves recognition but not VQA. 2. Dedicated vision capacity is key (4). An encoder-free model trails an encoder-based model on visual understanding, even when its backbone is enlarged by the encoders parameter count. The encoders advantage thus lies in capacity dedicated to vision rather than in total parameter count. 3. Vision capacity can move in-fusion (5). Adding vision-only capacity to the backbones earliest layers is comparable to adding from-scratch pre-fusion encoder. Scaling laws show in-fusion tracking the encoder, whereas encoder-free trails it at every size (5.4). 4. The findings hold beyond lifetime compute (6). Starting from pretrained 1.7B language model, in-fusion stays comparable to the from-scratch encoder while encoder-free falls further behind. In-fusion can also lower time to first token, since no separate encoder must run before the backbone. Together, these findings show that multimodal models benefit from dedicated vision capacity, which however needs neither separate pretraining nor pre-fusion placement.

sections.title: 2 A controlled protocol for comparing multimodal recipes
sections.content: We propose protocol that varies the three design choices vision encoder bundles, while holding fixed the data sources, optimization settings, compute, and backbone architecture. This isolates their effects when comparing current multimodal model recipes. Conclusions about these design choices cannot be drawn from comparing published models, because they differ in several factors at oncee.g., they build on different pretrained language models and vision encoders that each vary in training data and compute. We therefore use no external pretrained models: we train every component from scratch, with common data sources and training setups, and compare recipes at matched lifetime compute, the total compute of all training stages.

We describe how image patches reach the backbone relative to the multimodal fusion boundary, the first layer in which vision and text tokens can interact: vision-only computation before it is pre-fusion and computation inside the shared backbone is in-fusion (Figure 1 and Table 1). Scratch encoders ( ) process image patches pre-fusion with randomly initialized 27-layer, 0.4B-parameter Vision Transformer (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021; Alabdulmohsin et al., 2023) modeled after MoonViT-V2 (Kimi K3s encoder; Kimi Team, 2026b), whose output is linearly projected into the backbone. Pretrained encoders ( ) share this architecture, but we first pretrain them ourselves on our common data (Section 2.2) rather than taking external checkpoints. Encoder-free models ( ) map patches directly into the backbone with linear patch embedding (Adept AI, 2023; Gemma Team, 2026), followed by RMSNorm and learned scalar gate (Qi et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). In-fusion models ( ) instead add vision-only modules inside the backbone (Section 5). Every recipe trains on 224 224 images, read as 256 vision tokens using 14 14 patches. Instruction tuning for evaluation raises the resolution to 448 448 (1,024 vision tokens), as in PaliGemmas short high-resolution stage (Beyer et al., 2024), since OCR and chart reading needs fine detail (Tong et al., 2024a; Beyer, 2024).

sections.title: 2.2 Common data
sections.content: Text-only sequences come from Nemotron-CC v2/v2.1 (NVIDIA, 2025b,a), and imagetext sequences use MetaCLIP 1.2 pairs (English subset) (Xu et al., 2024). Encoder pretraining uses these pairs with their original alt-text, as in each objectives original setup (Section 3; e.g., CapPa, Tschannen et al., 2023), while multimodal training uses captions regenerated by Qwen2.5-VL-32B (Bai et al., 2025b) and shared by every recipe. Multimodal training mixes text-only and imagetext sequences 70:30, so recipes with pretrained encoder spend more lifetime compute on imagetext data. This matches the language share Han et al. (2026) found optimal and gave the best visual understanding in our sweep at small cost to text (Appendix A.4).

sections.title: 2.3 Lifetime compute
sections.content: Multimodal models often build on separately pretrained components whose training can even exceed the multimodal stage. For example, SigLIP 2, commonly used encoder, is trained on 40B imagetext sam4 ples (Tschannen et al., 2025), which translates to 10 trillion image tokens, while language models are typically also trained on trillions of text tokens (Touvron et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025). Counting only multimodal training therefore favors recipes that spend more compute in these earlier stages. To make such comparisons fair, we propose lifetime compute, the total training compute of every stage that produces the final model, Clifetime = sS Cs, (1) where is the set of training stages and Cs is the training compute of stage s. Here, contains multimodal training, any text-only training before it and, for pretrained encoders, encoder pretraining, but not instruction tuning. We report compute in FLOPs; because recipes differ in cost per token, matched compute means that they process different numbers of tokens. Appendix A.5 describes the compute accounting and converts each budget into token-equivalents, the number of tokens text-only model of the same size would process with the same compute. Lifetime compute models project that allocates one budget across every training stage, which lets us separate the contribution of each design choice. In practice, pretrained encoders are often available for free, so we also compare encoders with their pretraining compute not counted (Section 6.1).

sections.title: 2.4 Training schedule
sections.content: To compare recipes at many training lengths from one run (Zhai et al., 2022), we use warmupstabledecay schedule (Hu et al., 2024; Wen et al., 2025; Hägele et al., 2024), where the learning rate stays constant after warmup and any checkpoint of that run can be decayed to 5% of its peak over the final 10% of training (Appendix A.3). Our main comparisons span compute budgets from 6.5 1020 FLOPs, or 56B to 1.11T token-equivalents  (Table 12)  . We index budgets by tokens per parameter (TPP): token-equivalents divided by the backbones non-embedding parameters, i.e., all parameters except the tied token embedding (1.4B at 1.7B and 3.6B at 4B; backbones are named by their total parameters). Budgets reach 788 TPP at 1.7B and 306 TPP at 4B. All recipes share one peak learning rate per backbone size, scaled with the inverse square root of its total parameter count (3 10 at 4B). sections.title: 3 Does the vision encoder need separate pretraining?
sections.content: The first design choice vision encoder bundles is visual prior imported through separate pretraining, which recent models (Kimi Team, 2026b) forgo by training the encoder from scratch with the language model. Under fixed lifetime compute budget, encoder pretraining directly competes with multimodal training for FLOPs. Whether the prior is needed also shapes the remainder of our study, because encoder-free architectures cannot easily import one. We test whether the prior helps by comparing encoders pretrained with different objectives against the same encoder trained from scratch with the backbone. Setup. We pretrain separate encoder with each of four objectives and the same compute: contrastive imagetext alignment (MetaCLIP; Xu et al., 2024), self-supervised learning (WebSSL; Fan et al., 2025), and captioning (Cap and CapPa; Tschannen et al., 2023). sections.title: 4 Does vision encoding need dedicated capacity?
sections.content: The from-scratch encoder of Section 3 forgoes the imported prior but keeps the second design choice: dedicated vision capacity. Encoder-free models drop this capacity entirely and project image patches directly into the shared backbone (Adept AI, 2023; Diao et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2026; Gemma Team, 2026; Thinking Machines Lab, 2026a). Dropping the encoder, however, also removes substantial number of parameters and changes how raw patches enter the backbone, so gap between the two recipes could reflect fewer total parameters, weak patch embedding, or missing dedicated capacity. In this section, we test whether visual understanding needs this dedicated capacity, leaving the study of its precise placement to Section 5. Setup. We compare the from-scratch encoder (Section 3) with the encoder-free recipe (Section 2.1), which maps each patch into the backbone with linear patch embedding followed by RMSNorm and learned gate. As in every recipe, vision tokens attend to one another bidirectionally in the backbone (Section 2.1). sections.title: 5 Does dedicated capacity need to precede multimodal fusion?
sections.content: Section 4 shows that visual understanding benefits from dedicated capacity. We now ask whether that capacity must precede multimodal fusion. The encoders parameters are both dedicated, used only by vision tokens, and pre-fusion, processing vision tokens before they interact with text. We test whether pre-fusion placement is needed by moving the encoders parameter budget in-fusion, into vision-only modules inside the shared backbone (Section 5.1). Section 5.2 studies where this capacity should sit, which tokens should use it, and which modules it adds. Sections 5.3 and 5.4 then compare it with the encoder over training and with scale.

sections.title: 5.1 Moving the encoder’s capacity inside the backbone
sections.content: In-fusion vision capacity adds vision-only modules to selected backbone layers. In each of these layers, the attention projections and the feed-forward network (FFN) keep their shared weights and add vision-only counterparts, whose outputs add to the shared outputs after each module (Figure 4). Each vision-only module thus acts as an additive expert routed by modality: vision tokens use it alongside the shared weights. Unlike mixture-of-transformers (MoT; Liang et al., 2025), which gives text and vision tokens entirely separate parameters, in-fusion still passes every token through the shared parameters. Section 6.2 compares the two when starting from pretrained language models. sections.title: 5.2 Where and how to add in-fusion capacity
sections.content: We compare in-fusion designs that reallocate the encoders 0.4B vision parameters within the backbone. Placement of capacity within fusion. We study placement with the FFN-only variant, because FFN branches can be narrowed to fit any placement. Full-rank vision-only attention projections cannot, because adding them to every layer would take 88% of the 0.4B budget at 1.7B and exceed it at 4B. With the budget fixed, we compare four placements  (Table 3)  : narrow branch in every layer, or eight wider branches spread evenly across depth, in the last eight layers, or in the first eight layers. The first three variants do no better than the encoder-free model on Avg. VQA, whereas placing the modules in the first eight layers matches the scratch encoder. Early placement also helps most on OCR and chart questions, which depend on fine visual detail, whereas late placement does not. Dedicated in-fusion capacity is therefore most useful where the backbone first processes vision tokens, similar to an encoder. We hypothesize that vision tokens benefit most from vision-only processing while they are still close to raw patch features. Only early placement concentrates the budget there, whereas the every-layer and spread placements dilute it across the backbone. Layerwise representation similarity shows that the in-fusion models change vision tokens mostly within the first eight blocks, where their vision-only modules sit, and little afterward, while the encoder-free model keeps changing them through shared blocks 413 (Appendix E.4). Therefore, we use the first eight layers from here on. Reserving the capacity for vision tokens matters. To check that the gain comes from reserving this capacity for vision tokens, we also give the same parameters in the first eight layers to all tokens  (Table 3)  . Widening the shared FFNs barely improves over the encoder-free model. separate branch used by all tokens recovers some of the vision-only branchs gain, but still trails it even with twice the training  (Table 24)  . The all-token variants slightly improve on Avg. Text, because text also uses the added parameters. We hypothesize that vision-only branch gives vision tokens processing of their own without competing with text for the same parameters, while both still share the backbones attention and FFNs. Adding vision-only attention projections. With the capacity confined to the first eight layers, the QKVO attention projections fit within the budget (0.1B at 1.7B), so in-fusion adds them alongside narrower FFN branches. It is comparable to FFN-only at 1.7B and slightly ahead at every 4B budget (Figure 5), and its vision-only attention projections help on their own at 4B (Appendix E.2), so we use this variant as our default for the remainder of the paper.

In-fusion is comparable to the encoder throughout. Like the encoder, 9 Figure 5 In-fusion is comparable to FFN-only at 1.7B and slightly ahead at every 4B budget. Part of the in-fusion budget sits in vision-only attention projections, which help on their own in additional 4B ablations (Appendix E.2). Dedicated vision capacity therefore does not need to precede fusion to benefit visual understanding. In-fusion can also lower time to first token for image requests, since no encoder runs before the backbone (Section 6.3).

sections.content: So far, we have compared the recipes at 1.7B and 4B with 0.4B of dedicated vision capacity. To see how they behave with scale, we train them on ladder of five backbone sizes from 0.6B to 6.4B (setup in Appendix G). The dedicated vision capacity grows with the backbone, keeping its share of parameters from the 1.7B model, as in jointly scaled models (Chen et al., 2023; Tian et al., 2025). For each recipe, we fit Avg. VQA, caption loss, and text loss as functions of model size and token-equivalents on all of its ladder runs. sections.title: 6 Vision encoding beyond lifetime compute
sections.content: Our main investigations (Sections 3 to 5) are deliberately controlled: they train every component from scratch and charge each stages compute to one lifetime budget, which enables us to isolate the three design choices of vision encoder. In practice, however, multimodal models are often built from separately pretrained components: language model and, usually, vision encoder. Inference speed for serving also shapes these design decisions. We find that free pretrained encoder still does not help backbone trained from scratch (Section 6.1), and that instead midtraining 1.7B text-only model leaves the comparisons of Sections 3 to 5 unchanged (Section 6.2). Finally, in-fusion can lower the time to first token for image requests (Section 6.3).

sections.title: 6.1 Zero-cost pretrained encoders
sections.content: Section 3 charges encoder pretraining to the lifetime budget, but in practice pretrained encoder is often available for free. Here, we hold multimodal training fixed at 2.7 1021 FLOPs and vary MetaCLIP pretraining from 1.4 1021 FLOPs. This raises the encoders ImageNet linear-probe accuracy before multimodal training from 80.4% to 84.4% (Figure 8; Appendix C.3), yet Avg. VQA is highest after the shortest pretraining, and an encoder trained from scratch with the same multimodal training matches it. Thus, even when pretraining is free, more of it does not help. to 9.

sections.title: 6.2 Midtraining from pretrained language models
sections.content: Many multimodal models add vision to language model pretrained on text alone (Alayrac et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023; Tong et al., 2024a; Bai et al., 2025a). We call this stage of continued training on multimodal data midtraining. We test whether the comparisons of Sections 3 to 5 hold in this setting. We pretrain our own 1.7B language model on 1T tokens of the same text data and then midtrain it to 1.33T token-equivalents with each recipe at equal compute (Figure 9). Following DeepSeek-VL (Lu et al., 2024a), midtraining keeps 70% text data; as in Section 6.1, MetaCLIPs encoder pretraining is not counted. Besides the four recipes, we compare MoT (Section 5.1, initialized from the language model) and variant that copies only its first eight layers, matching the encoders 0.4B vision-only parameters. In-fusion, MoT layers 18, and the from-scratch encoder perform comparably, and all lead encoder-free. The full MoT model falls behind despite 3.5 times as many vision-only parametersadding vision-only copies of the later layers to MoT layers 18 hurts, consistent with late placement not helping in Section 5.2. free MetaCLIP encoder, which matches the from-scratch encoder when the backbone is also trained from scratch (Section 6.1), trails it here, mostly on OCR, chart, and vision-centric questions. Tuning each encoders learning rate does not change these conclusions (Appendix H.1). We hypothesize that the from-scratch encoder learns features suited to the pretrained language model from its first update, whereas MetaCLIPs contrastive features, which miss fine visual detail (Tong et al., 2024b), must be reshaped by language model that already leans on text. Every recipe keeps Avg. Text within point of text-only control. Thus, the conclusions from our controlled experiments (Sections 3 to 5) carry over to midtraining, where free pretrained encoder trails the from-scratch encoder, encoder-free trails on VQA, and in-fusion is comparable to the pre-fusion encoder.

sections.title: 6.3 Training and inference speed
sections.content: A separate encoder must finish processing each image before the backbone can start, which adds serial step to inference. Following the inference benchmark of Mono-InternVL (Luo et al., 2025b), we measure time to first token (TTFT) on one H200 with 16 concurrent requests, each with one 448-pixel image and 256 text tokens (Appendix H.3). At 1.7B with 0.4B vision-only parameters, in-fusion and its FFN-only variant are clearly faster than the encoder (Figure 10) at comparable Avg. VQA  (Table 26)  . MoT, which copies the first backbone layers for vision tokens, is about as fast as in-fusion up to 0.4B vision-only parameters, but its added TTFT grows faster with the budget, while staying below the encoders TTFT. Encoder-free is fastest but clearly trails on Avg. VQA  (Table 26)  . In-fusions TTFT advantage over the encoder grows with the vision-only budget (Figure 10), which scales with the backbone (Section 5.4); at fixed budget, vision adds nearly the same time at 1.7B and 4B  (Table 36)  . Earlier encoder-free models report larger TTFT reductions, up to 69% (Luo et al., 2025b,a), although their gains also reflect other efficiency changes. Inference benefits also depend on deployment details. Under continuous batching of mixed text and image requests, in-fusions vision-only modules run in the same forward passes as text-only requests, whereas separate encoder adds latency only to image requests. Finally, both in-fusion variants train as fast as encoder-free, whereas the encoder recipe is 3% slower at 4B  (Table 35)  . Figure 10 In-fusion serves images faster than the encoder at every vision parameter budget. Designs are parameter-matched on the 1.7B backbone. Takeaway 4: Our findings hold beyond lifetime compute, and in-fusion can be faster to serve. free pretrained encoder still does not help, the comparisons carry over to midtraining, and in-fusion lowers TTFT at comparable VQA.

sections.title: 7 Related work
sections.content: Multimodal model recipes. Most multimodal models connect separately pretrained vision encoder (Radford et al., 2021; Tschannen et al., 2025; Bolya et al., 2025), kept frozen (Liu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023b; Muse Glimmer Team, 2026) or updated (Beyer et al., 2024; Steiner et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2025a), to pretrained language model. More recent models train the encoder from scratch with the language model (Kimi Team, 2026b; Tian et al., 2025), embed image patches without an encoder (Adept AI, 2023; Diao et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Gemma Team, 2026; Thinking Machines Lab, 2026a), or quantize images with separately trained tokenizer (Chameleon Team, 2024; Wang et al., 2026). Inkling was released as encoder-free, yet its successor, Inkling 2 Small, uses 292M-parameter vision encoder (Thinking Machines Lab, 2026a,b). Because these models also differ in data, pretrained components, and compute, comparing them directly does not isolate single design choice. We therefore train every stage of each recipe class from scratch on common data sources and compare the recipes at matched lifetime compute (Section 2). Controlled studies. Prior controlled studies of encoder pretraining typically start from pretrained language model, count only multimodal training, and compare encoder pretraining objectives and data (Karamcheti et al., 2024; McKinzie et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2024a; Laurençon et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025) rather than studying whether separate pretraining is needed at all. The few works that compare pretrained and from-scratch encoders vary in their findings, possibly because they control neither the encoders pretraining data nor lifetime compute (Tian et al., 2025; Kimi Team, 2026b). Studies raise similar question for language pretraining, finding that adding vision before text-only pretraining ends, rather than after it, improves visual understanding (Keh et al., 2025; Han et al., 2026; Kimi Team, 2026a), as in our delayed-vision experiments  (Table 11)  . Encoder pretraining also confounds encoder vs. encoder-free comparisons, which typically pit pretrained encoder against an encoder-free model (Beyer et al., 2024; Diao et al., 2024; Lei et al., 2025; Diao et al., 2025; Tong et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026). Such comparisons remove separate pretraining, dedicated capacity, and pre-fusion placement at once, and often attribute the encoders advantage to pretraining data they do not control. Shukor et al. (2025), who train both designs from scratch, find that encoder-free models match or slightly outperform an encoder. In contrast, we find that the encoder leads on VQA and held-out caption loss, which we trace to their setup (Appendix D.4). 12 Dedicated vision capacity. Testing whether dedicated capacity must precede fusion requires moving the encoders capacity inside the backbone, which the encoder vs. encoder-free comparisons cannot accomplish. Prior works on fusion depth come closer, varying where modalities begin to interact (Nagrani et al., 2021; Hao et al., 2026) or where encoder features enter the backbone (Meng et al., 2024), but none moves fixed amount of vision-only capacity into layers that vision and text share. Other multimodal architectures add vision-specific parameters to the backbone, but not in form that fits this comparison. Modality-expert designs duplicate the backbones weights for vision tokens, typically in every layer, and route vision tokens through these copies instead of the shared weights (Bao et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2025). Their vision-only capacity is thus set by the backbones size and spread over its depth rather than held at an encoders budget early in the model, and most also build on pretrained language model (Wang et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2025b; Tian et al., 2025; Diao et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2025). Adapter architectures fine-tune pretrained model through small parallel or low-rank modules shared by all tokens (He et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2022; Hu et al., 2022), and their multimodal variants keep an encoder alongside the adapters (Dong et al., 2024; Shapourian et al., 2026) or distill from one (Wang et al., 2025). The encoders in these works still supply pre-fusion capacity or pretrained prior, the two factors our comparison aims to remove. We instead give vision tokens their own attention projections and feed-forward branches in selected backbone layers. Their outputs add to the shared ones and together match an encoders parameter budget, so only the placement of this capacity changes (Section 5). Placed in the first eight layers, in-fusion capacity is comparable to pre-fusion encoder on VQA, so dedicated vision capacity helps whether it sits pre-fusion or in-fusion.

sections.title: 8 Discussion
sections.content: With multimodal models revisiting the vision encoder, we asked which of its design choices are still beneficial. We proposed unbundling the encoder into three choices: visual prior from separate pretraining, dedicated vision capacity, and pre-fusion placement of that capacity. We tested each by training every recipe from scratch on common data, with one architecture and optimization setup, and comparing recipes on text and visual understanding benchmarks at matched lifetime compute. Takeaways from unbundling. Of the three choices an encoder bundles, only dedicated vision capacity maintains its advantage. Separate pretraining is unnecessary: an encoder trained jointly with the backbone is on par with pretrained ones, and longer pretraining improves recognition but not VQA, even when it is free (Sections 3 and 6.1). Dedicated capacity matters: with the encoders parameters added to their shared backbone, encoder-free models gain on Avg. Text but still trail the encoder on Avg. VQA (Section 4), most on OCR and chart questions  (Table 2)  . This capacity belongs early, but it need not precede the backbone: vision-only modules in the first backbone layers are comparable to pre-fusion encoder (Section 5). For recipes that drop the encoder, this suggests reallocating its parameters as vision-only capacity in the earliest layers rather than as shared parameters. Limitations and future work. To keep comparisons controlled, we pretrain encoders on the same images as multimodal training, so our results do not rule out benefit from released encoders trained on additional data. Encoder pretraining uses the images original alt-text, as in standard imagetext pretraining; pretraining on our regenerated captions instead changes little  (Table 9)  . Our experiments are on dense backbones with up to 6.4B parameters; the most compelling next step is extending them to sparse mixture-of-experts backbones, whose experts could naturally host in-fusions modality-routed capacity. Multimodal training also uses 224 224 MetaCLIP images, leaving higher-resolution training and more text-rich data to future work. The textimage data mixture was selected with the from-scratch encoder at 1.7B, so mixtures tuned for each recipe remain underexplored (Appendix A.4). Finally, how architecture interacts with interleaved imagetext and video data remains open. Conclusion. We presented controlled study that disentangles the design choices behind how multimodal models process visual input, studying each choice in isolation instead of as part of bundled recipe. Rather than assembling multimodal models from components optimized for different objectives, our findings favor training them end-to-end as one system.

sections.title: A Controlled protocol
sections.content: Unless stated otherwise, every comparison of the 1.7B and 4B backbones uses the settings below, which detail the protocol of Section 2. A.1 Architectures The multimodal recipes differ in where their vision-only capacity sits and how it is trained: in pre-fusion vision encoder that is pretrained and then frozen or updated, or trained from scratch, encoder-free with no module besides patch embedding, or vision-only modules inside the shared backbone (in-fusion vision capacity; Appendix E.1). Unless variable is the stated ablation, comparisons hold the backbone, the 256 vision tokens per image in multimodal training, the data, the optimization recipe, and lifetime compute fixed. Table 4 lists the backbone and encoder architectures. Backbone. The shared backbone is dense decoder-only Transformer that follows the Qwen3-1.7B and Its FFNs use Qwen3-4B configurations (Yang et al., 2025) and is trained from random initialization. SwiGLU (Shazeer, 2020), and its attention uses grouped keyvalue heads with RMSNorm on queries and keys. The vision-only FFN branches of in-fusion vision capacity use the same form and read the same normalized input as the shared FFN (Appendix E.1). Vision encoder. The encoder follows MoonViT-V2, the vision encoder of Kimi K3 (Kimi Team, 2026b), in depth, patch size, normalization, and size: 27 layers, patch size 14, RMSNorm, and about 0.4B parameters in total. It has width 1,024 with 4,096-wide MLPs and uses learned spatial position embeddings combined with interleaved two-dimensional rotary position embeddings. During multimodal training, each image is resized bilinearly to shorter side of 224 pixels, center-cropped to 224 224, and divided into 14 14 patches, producing 256 vision tokens. For an image x, the encoder recipe computes venc(x) = Wprojfϕ(x), (4) where fϕ is the vision encoder and the linear projector Wproj maps its output width to the backbone width. Pretrained variants (Section 3) use the same architecture and differ only in the pretraining objective. MetaCLIP and WebSSL use class token during upstream training; we discard it and pass only the 256 patch tokens to the backbone (Liu et al., 2023). 21 Table 4 Every multimodal recipe shares one backbone configuration per scale, and the encoder adds 0.4B ViT. Parameter counts exclude the linear projection from the encoder into the backbone. Backbone Vision encoder 1.7B 4B 0.4B Configuration Layers Width Query heads FFN width Tied embeddings Parameters (B) Non-embedding parameters (B) Qwen3-1.7B Qwen3-4B 28 2,048 16 6,144 1.72 1.41 36 2,560 32 9,728 4.02 3.63 MoonViT-V2 27 1,024 12 4,096 0.40 Keyvalue heads Head dimension FFN activation Normalization Position encoding Input Tokens Shared 8 128 SwiGLU RMSNorm 1D RoPE 152K-token vocabulary 4,096 per sequence 12 128 GELU RMSNorm learned 2D + 2D RoPE 14 14 patches 256 per image Encoder-free patch embedding. The encoder-free recipe projects each flattened 14 14 RGB patch linearly into the backbone width, as in Fuyu and Gemma 4 (Adept AI, 2023; Gemma Team, 2026), and applies RMSNorm and learned scalar gate (Qi et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026), giving 256 backbone tokens per image: vfree(x) = RMSNorm (Wpatch Patchify(x) + p2D) , (5) where p2D is fixed two-dimensional sinecosine position embedding and the learned scalar gate is initialized to 0.1. The in-fusion models of Appendix E.1 use the same patch embedding. A.2 Encoder design selection We chose the from-scratch encoders shape and size at matched lifetime compute, and every main comparison uses the resulting 27-layer, 0.4B encoder. The shape and size comparisons use the 1.7B backbone at 2.6 1021 FLOPs  (Table 5)  . The configurations in Table 5 vary the structure of the dedicated visual computation. Half-Depth, Wide, and Shallow + Wide are pre-fusion encoders that change the default encoders depth, width, or both. The backbone-style encoder is also pre-fusion encoder. It has its own patch embedding and eight Transformer blocks shaped like those of the 1.7B backbone, and it connects to the backbone through the linear projection of Equation 4. The Default, Shallow + Wide, and backbone-style variants use about the same vision-only parameter budget; the Half-Depth and Wide variants test smaller and larger budgets, respectively. The Size section of Table 5 scales the default encoders depth and width together, from Small (0.05B) to Huge (0.92B). At matched lifetime compute, encoders with more parameters process fewer tokens. The default encoder is comparable to Wide on VQA while using fewer vision-only parameters. Avg. Text does not follow encoder size: Small and Huge score highest, and the default slightly lower. At 4B. We further ablate encoder size at the 4B model scale, using the same from-scratch recipe  (Table 6)  . The default Large encoder is strongest on both Avg. Text and Avg. VQA. At both scales, the default encoder gives the highest Avg. VQA, and Avg. Text does not follow encoder size. At 6.4B. On the 6.4B backbone of the size ladder (Appendix G), we also keep the 0.4B encoder instead of scaling it to 1.7B with the backbone. sections.title: B Evaluation
sections.content: This section describes the two main evaluation metrics, Avg. VQA and Avg. Text. We also define the held-out losses that Sections 4 and 5.4 and Appendix F.3 use as well as two additional metrics, out-of-distribution caption loss and ImageNet linear-probe accuracy. B.1 VQA benchmarks Visual instruction tuning. We use instruction tuning as an evaluation protocol (Tong et al., 2024a). Every multimodal model checkpoint is instruction-tuned with one fixed recipe before we measure its visual understanding. The recipe runs three epochs of Cambrian-7M (Tong et al., 2024a) before evaluation. Multimodal training reads 224 224 images, but instruction tuning and evaluation raise the resolution to 26 448 448 (1,024 vision tokens), since OCR and chart reading needs fine detail (Tong et al., 2024a; Beyer, 2024). Exhibits whose captions say so instead retain the multimodal-training resolution of 224 224 (256 vision tokens), otherwise with the same recipe. The encoders learned position table is interpolated to the larger patch grid, and the fixed sinecosine positions of encoder-free and in-fusion models are recomputed for it. Cambrian-7M is curated instruction-tuning mixture spanning general visual tasks, OCR and charts, counting, math, science, code, and language-only data. Table 8 provides the optimizer settings and batch size. Instruction tuning updates the same parameters as multimodal training. Therefore, frozen encoder, e.g., the frozen MetaCLIP encoder in Table 16, stays frozen. Benchmarks and Avg. VQA. Evaluation follows the Cambrian-1 visual understanding suite (Tong et al., 2024a), using greedy decoding with at most 256 output tokens. Each task is capped at its first 5,000 examples in dataset order. Table 13 lists the 16 benchmarks in four categories (general, knowledge, OCR and chart, and vision-centric), with the split, metric, and number of examples for each. Exact match compares the normalized parsed answer or option letter with the reference answers, relaxed accuracy tolerates small numeric errors, and VQA accuracy is the consensus metric (Antol et al., 2015) that TextVQA uses. Each category mean averages its four benchmarks. The suite contains 15 benchmarks scored in [0, 100] and MME-Perception (MME-P), whose ten subtasks each score out of 200. We divide the MME-P total by 20 to put it on the same scale, and Avg. VQA is the mean of the 16 scores, which equals the mean of the four category means. Table 13 Avg. The held-out text and caption losses score unseen samples of the training distributions, and Sections 4 and 5.4 28 and Appendix F.3 use them. Out-of-distribution caption loss scores caption sets outside those distributions, and Table 25 reports it. In-distribution. Held-out text loss is the per-token negative log-likelihood on held-out text from the training text corpus, weighted as in the training mixture. It is scored with the attention masking each model was trained with. Held-out caption loss is the per-token negative log-likelihood of the regenerated captions of MetaCLIP 1.2 images never used in training, so it samples the training caption distribution. Out-of-distribution. Out-of-distribution caption loss averages the caption loss of three sets of 5,000 images with equal weight: the COCO validation images with the first of their human reference captions (Lin et al., 2014), MetaCLIP 1.2 pairs with their original alt-text (Xu et al., 2024), and images from licensed stock-photo collection. It is scored with the attention masking each model was trained with. B.5 ImageNet linear probes 4, 10 We use three linear probes on ImageNet-1K (Deng et al., 2009). The downstream probe reads the multimodal model with all weights frozen. It mean-pools the backbones final normalized vision-token states and fits an ℓ2-regularized linear classifier on 50 training images per class. fixed 10% holdout selects the regularization strength from {10 }, and the classifier is then refit on all 50,000 images. We report top-1 accuracy on the full validation split. The upstream probe  (Table 16)  fits the same classifier to frozen pretrained encoder before multimodal training. It mean-pools the encoders 256 final normalized patch tokens of 224 224 center crop; for WebSSL, it reads the exponential-moving-average teacher. The full-data probe applies the DINOv2 linear evaluation (Oquab et al., 2024) to the frozen pretrained encoder, training on the full ImageNet-1K training set. sections.content: Section 5.4 tests whether the comparisons of Sections 4 and 5 hold as the backbone grows, using ladder of backbone sizes. This section gives the ladders setup, the scaling laws fitted to it, and how well the laws predict runs they were not fitted on. Setup. The ladder trains the encoder-free, encoder, and in-fusion recipes under the protocol of Section 2 on backbones from 0.6B to 6.4B parameters. The backbones follow the architecture of the 1.7B backbone, with query heads of dimension 128 spanning the hidden size, half as many keyvalue heads, and feed-forward width three times the hidden size. The vision module grows with the backbone  (Table 28)  . The encoder keeps the proportions of the 1.7B pairing: half the backbones hidden size d, one layer fewer than the backbone, an MLP four times its own width, and round(0.75 d/128) attention heads of dimension 128. Its parameter count therefore stays at nearly fixed ratio to the backbones non-embedding parameters. The in-fusion modules occupy the first round(8L/28) of the backbones layers, 29% of the depth, as at 1.7B. Their widths are set so that they match the encoders parameter count. 4 All recipes at backbone size share one peak learning rate and one batch size  (Table 28)  . The peak learning rate is 3 10 1.72 109/Ntot, rounded, where Ntot is the total backbone parameter count. The batch size grows by about 1.5 times per backbone size. Warmup lasts 2 tokens per non-embedding backbone parameter (2 TPP), e.g., 2.8B tokens for the 1.7B backbone, which has 1.4B non-embedding parameters. The other settings follow Table 8. The 1.7B and 4B runs of Sections 3 to 5 instead keep batch of 1,024 sequences and 4,000 warmup updates at both sizes.
